subject: Business
title: Bonds: Lending Money for Interest
description: A micro-lesson that makes Bonds: Lending Money for Interest usable.

hook.text: When you buy a US Treasury bond, you're lending money to the government. They pay you back with interest.

buildup.text: A bond is an IOU: the issuer borrows your money, pays regular interest (coupon), and returns principal at maturity.

discovery.text: Bonds are rated from AAA (safest) to junk. Higher risk bonds pay higher interest to attract buyers.

twist.text: When interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall. Investors sell old bonds yielding less for new ones yielding more.

climax.text: In 2022, bonds lost 13% — the worst year since 1842 — as the Fed rapidly raised rates.

punchline.text: Bonds are safe until interest rates move. Then they're a reminder that 'safe' is relative.

quiz.question: What happens to existing bond prices when interest rates rise?
options: Existing bond prices fall because new bonds offer higher yields
Bond prices rise with interest rates
Bond prices are unaffected by interest rate changes

details.summary: Bonds are loans you make to governments or corporations in exchange for regular interest payments and the return of your principal at maturity. They are generally less volatile than stocks and provide predictable income streams for conservative investors.
details.whyItMatters: Bonds offer stability and income in a diversified portfolio. Understanding how bond prices move inversely with interest rates helps investors make better allocation decisions during different economic cycles.
takeaways: Bondholders lend money and receive fixed interest payments called coupons
Bond prices fall when interest rates rise and vice versa
Government bonds are safer while corporate bonds offer higher yields

faq.question: Why do bond prices move opposite to interest rates?
faq.answer: When new bonds offer higher rates, existing bonds with lower rates become less attractive. Investors will only buy them at a discount. Conversely, when rates drop, existing bonds paying higher rates become more valuable, pushing their prices up.

faq.question: Are bonds risk-free investments?
faq.answer: No. Bonds carry interest rate risk, credit risk if the issuer defaults, and inflation risk if returns fail to keep up with rising prices. Government bonds from stable nations are among the safest but still lose purchasing power if inflation exceeds the coupon rate.
